name: Kala Patthar
tagline: The 5,644 m viewpoint with the closest full view of Everest's summit
meta_description: Kala Patthar (5,644 m): the highest point of the Everest Base Camp trek, a 2–3 hour climb from Gorak Shep for the full view of Everest, Nuptse and Lhotse.
summary: Kala Patthar is a brown rocky ridge below Pumori, rising to 5,644 m above Gorak Shep. It is the highest point of most Everest treks and the best place to see the whole south-west face of Everest, from the Khumbu Icefall to the summit, usually climbed before dawn in 2–3 hours.
intro: Kala Patthar means black rock in Nepali, and the name fits: it is a dark, scree-covered spur running south from Pumori (7,161 m), standing above the sandy basin of Gorak Shep. From its crest, Everest appears in full, closer and higher than anywhere else trekkers can reach. You see the summit pyramid, the South Col, the Lhotse face, the Western Cwm's exit and the Khumbu Icefall below, with Nuptse's long ridge to the right and Changtse peeking from Tibet.

The usual plan is to climb from Gorak Shep (5,164 m) before dawn, starting around 4:30 to 5 am with headlamps, to reach the top as the sun lights Everest from behind. The climb gains about 480 m over roughly 2 km, first on a sandy path across the dry lake bed and then on steady zigzags up the grassy and rocky slope. Most trekkers take 2 to 3 hours up and about an hour down. The final few metres to the highest summit block are a scramble over boulders hung with prayer flags.

Some groups climb Kala Patthar in the late afternoon instead, after visiting base camp in the morning, when the sun sets behind them and lights the face of Everest. Both work; mornings are usually clearer and calmer, afternoons warmer but cloudier. Kala Patthar is also a helicopter landing point on many Everest heli tours, landing on the ridge for a short stop when weather and current rules allow. Either way, it is the photograph most people came for.
facts: Lukla, 8–9 days' walk; heli landings on the ridge when permitted
≈ 35 min flight to Lukla + 8–9 days' walk, or ≈ 1.5 h by helicopter
Full view of Everest, highest point of the EBC trek

highlights.title: Everest summit in full view
highlights.text: From the top you see Everest from the Khumbu Icefall to the summit, with the South Col, Lhotse face and the line of the South-East Ridge used by most climbers. It is about 8 km away in a straight line.

highlights.title: Sunrise light on the Himalaya
highlights.text: At dawn the sun rises behind Everest, so the summit glows while the Khumbu below is still dark. Within minutes Nuptse, Lhotse, Ama Dablam to the south and Pumori above you turn gold and pink.

highlights.title: Pumori towering above
highlights.text: Pumori (7,161 m) rises directly behind Kala Patthar, its icy pyramid filling the sky to the north. The name means unmarried daughter, reportedly given by George Mallory. From the summit block you see its ice cliffs at close range.

highlights.title: Khumbu Glacier from above
highlights.text: Looking east from the ridge, the Khumbu Glacier curves from the icefall past base camp and down the valley in grey rubble and white seracs. In spring you can make out expedition tents as coloured dots on the ice.

highlights.title: Highest point of the trek
highlights.text: At 5,644 m, Kala Patthar is higher than base camp and the high point of the classic EBC trek. For many trekkers it is the highest they have ever stood, and the prayer flags at the top mark the moment.

highlights.title: Helicopter landing ridge
highlights.text: Many Everest heli tours land on the Kala Patthar ridge for 10–15 minutes, weather and current landing rules permitting. It is the highest point most helicopter guests set foot on, with the same face-on view of Everest.

how_to_reach.text: From Gorak Shep (5,164 m) a clear trail climbs about 480 m to the top in 2–3 hours, returning in about an hour. To reach Gorak Shep from Lukla takes about 8 days on the standard itinerary via Namche, Tengboche, Dingboche and Lobuche.

Helicopter tours from Kathmandu or Lukla land on the ridge at about 5,550 m for 10–15 minutes, weather permitting, then descend to Hotel Everest View for breakfast. At this height helicopters carry fewer passengers, so groups may be flown in two shuttles. Landing rules change; check current status before you travel.
Fixed-wing flights reach only Lukla (2,860 m), about 35 minutes from Kathmandu or 20 minutes from Ramechhap in peak months. From there the walk to Kala Patthar takes 8 days with acclimatisation.

where_to_stay: There is no accommodation on Kala Patthar. You sleep at Gorak Shep (5,164 m), at the foot of the climb, where a handful of basic lodges offer twin rooms with thin walls, shared toilets and a heated dining room. Rooms are cold, food prices are the highest on the trail, and water is limited, so most people stay one night only. Lobuche (4,940 m), 2–3 hours down the valley, has more lodges and a slightly better night's sleep. On the way down after Kala Patthar, most groups walk to Pheriche (4,371 m) or Dingboche, where the thicker air helps recovery.
tips: Start the sunrise climb by 5 am in October and November, with a full headlamp battery and water in an insulated bottle.
Wear every warm layer you have, including down jacket, hat, gloves and spare mitts: dawn on the ridge is often −15 °C with wind.
Go at your own pace; the view from the lower viewpoint at about 5,550 m is nearly as good if you need to stop early.
Keep phone and camera batteries warm in an inner pocket, as cold drains them fast.
If you have a bad headache, vomiting or confusion, do not climb; descend with your guide instead.

experiences.title: Kala Patthar sunrise climb
experiences.summary: Leave Gorak Shep by headlamp around 4:30 to 5 am, climb about 480 m on a zigzag trail, and reach the prayer flags at 5,644 m as the sun rises behind Everest. It is the high point of the classic trek.
body: Your guide wakes you at about 4 am with tea. In October and November it is around −12 to −15 °C outside, so dress fully inside the lodge: base layers, fleece, down jacket, windproof shell, hat, buff, liner gloves and mitts. Carry a litre of water in an insulated bottle, a chocolate bar and a camera. The first 20 minutes cross the sandy lake bed of Gorak Shep, then the trail begins to climb in steady switchbacks up the slope below Pumori.

The climb is not technical, but at this height every step is slow, and many trekkers find themselves stopping every few metres to breathe. That is normal. About two thirds of the way up, a broad shoulder at roughly 5,550 m gives an excellent view and is a sensible stopping point if you are tired or the wind is strong. The true top is a small rocky summit with prayer flags, reached by a short scramble over boulders.

As the sky lightens, Everest is backlit and its summit catches the first sun, followed by Nuptse, Lhotse and Ama Dablam to the south. Stay 15–30 minutes, take your photographs and come down before you get too cold. Back at Gorak Shep for breakfast at around 8 am, you pack and walk down to Pheriche or Dingboche the same day. The descent alone usually makes everyone feel better.

faqs.q: How long does it take to climb Kala Patthar?
faqs.a: Most trekkers take 2–3 hours to climb from Gorak Shep to the summit and about 1 hour to come down. Fit, well-acclimatised walkers may manage it in 1.5 hours. Start early enough to arrive around sunrise, typically 5:45 to 6:15 am in October and November.

faqs.q: Is Kala Patthar harder than Everest Base Camp?
faqs.a: Yes, for most people. It gains about 480 m from Gorak Shep in one push to 5,644 m, compared with the mostly level moraine walk to base camp. The trail is not technical, but the altitude, early start and cold make it the toughest few hours of the trek.

faqs.q: Should I climb Kala Patthar at sunrise or sunset?
faqs.a: Sunrise is usually clearer and calmer, and most groups climb then. Sunset gives warmer light on Everest's face but higher odds of cloud. If you visit base camp in the morning, a late-afternoon climb can work. Your guide will decide based on weather and how you feel.

experiences.title: Late-afternoon Kala Patthar for sunset light
experiences.price_hint: Included in our EBC treks when weather suits
experiences.summary: On settled days, climbing Kala Patthar in the late afternoon puts the setting sun behind you and lights the west face of Everest orange and red. It suits strong groups who reach Gorak Shep early.
body: In the morning sunrise climb, Everest is backlit and its face is in shadow. In the late afternoon the light comes from the west, behind Kala Patthar, so the entire south-west face of Everest, the Lhotse wall and Nuptse catch direct sun. As the sun drops, the snow turns gold, then orange, then a deep rose colour, and the summit is often the last thing still lit while Gorak Shep falls into darkness.

The catch is weather. In the trekking seasons, cloud often builds over the Khumbu after midday and may clear again only by evening, so a sunset climb is a gamble. It works best in late October, November and December, when afternoons are more often clear, and on days when you reach Gorak Shep from Lobuche by 11 am. Some groups visit base camp the next morning instead, swapping the usual order.

Going up at 3 pm and coming down in the last light means descending the final half hour by headlamp, which is fine on this clear trail with a guide but very cold. Carry the same warm layers as for sunrise, plus a spare battery. If the sky is grey at 2 pm, rest and go at dawn instead. In either case, one ascent of Kala Patthar is enough, and the sunrise option remains the reliable choice.

faqs.q: Is sunset on Kala Patthar better than sunrise?
faqs.a: For photography, sunset often gives warmer front light on Everest's face, while sunrise backlights it. But afternoons are cloudier, so the chance of a clear view is lower. Most guides prefer sunrise for reliability and suggest sunset only on clear, settled afternoons.

faqs.q: Is it safe to come down Kala Patthar in the dark?
faqs.a: With a guide, a good headlamp and warm clothes, the last 30–45 minutes of descent in the dark is manageable, because the trail is wide and well used. Do not go alone, keep together, and turn around early if the wind is strong or anyone feels unwell.

faqs.q: Can I do Kala Patthar and Everest Base Camp on the same day?
faqs.a: Strong, well-acclimatised trekkers sometimes visit base camp in the morning from Gorak Shep and climb Kala Patthar for sunset. It is a long, tiring day at over 5,100 m. Most itineraries split them over the afternoon and the next morning.

experiences.title: Land on Kala Patthar by helicopter
experiences.duration: 10–15 minutes on the ridge (4–5 h tour)
experiences.price_hint: From ≈ US$ 1,190 per seat on a shared tour
experiences.summary: On our Everest heli tour, the helicopter lands on the Kala Patthar ridge at about 5,550 m for a short stop facing Everest, weather and current landing rules permitting, then descends to Hotel Everest View for breakfast.
body: The helicopter leaves Kathmandu at around 6:30 am, refuels at Lukla, then flies up the Dudh Koshi past Namche and Tengboche and along the Khumbu valley. After about 20–25 minutes from Lukla it lands on a flat area on the Kala Patthar ridge at around 5,550 m. You step out into thin, cold air with Everest, Nuptse and the Khumbu Icefall in front of you. The pilot keeps the rotor turning and stays in the aircraft.

Time on the ground is short, usually 10 to 15 minutes, because the human body has not acclimatised and symptoms of altitude sickness can start quickly at this height. Move slowly, do not run or climb, and get back in when the crew calls. Helicopters can carry fewer passengers at this altitude, so a full five-seat group may be split, with some guests waiting at Pheriche or Lukla while the first group lands. The crew may carry oxygen.

Landing depends on weather, wind and the rules in force. Clouds often build by 10 or 11 am, so tours leave early. If a landing on Kala Patthar is not possible, the pilot may land lower, at Gorak Shep or elsewhere, or fly past base camp without landing. Anyone with heart or lung disease, uncontrolled blood pressure, recent surgery or pregnancy should not land above 5,000 m, and young children should stay lower.

faqs.q: Do Everest helicopter tours land on Kala Patthar?
faqs.a: Many do, on the ridge at around 5,550 m, when weather and current landing rules allow. If landing is not permitted or conditions are poor, pilots land at another point such as Gorak Shep or fly over without landing. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How long can you stay at Kala Patthar on a heli tour?
faqs.a: Usually 10–15 minutes. Without acclimatisation, staying longer at about 5,500 m raises the risk of headache, nausea and dizziness. The crew decides the exact time based on how passengers feel and the weather.

faqs.q: Who should not land at Kala Patthar?
faqs.a: People with heart or lung conditions, severe high blood pressure, anaemia, recent surgery or pregnancy, and infants. They can join the tour and stay in the helicopter or wait at a lower point. Consult your doctor before booking if you have any medical condition.

The summit of Kala Patthar is about 5,644 m above sea level, roughly 480 m above Gorak Shep and higher than Everest Base Camp at about 5,364 m. The main viewpoint below the summit block is at around 5,550 m, which is also where helicopters land.

faqs.q: Is Kala Patthar worth it after Everest Base Camp?
faqs.a: Yes. Base camp lacks a view of Everest's summit; Kala Patthar shows the whole mountain from the icefall to the top, plus Nuptse, Lhotse and Pumori. Most trekkers say it is the best view of the entire trek, so we include it in every EBC itinerary.

Yes, if they are well acclimatised after 8 days on the trail. No climbing skills are needed, only walking poles and patience. The challenge is the altitude and cold, not technique. Anyone with symptoms of altitude sickness should skip it and descend.

faqs.q: What is the temperature on Kala Patthar at sunrise?
faqs.a: In October and November, expect about −12 to −18 °C at dawn with wind chill, rising quickly once the sun hits the ridge. In April and May it is around −8 to −12 °C. Winter dawns can drop below −20 °C.

faqs.q: How far is Kala Patthar from Everest?
faqs.a: The summit of Kala Patthar is about 8 km in a straight line from the summit of Everest, across the Khumbu Glacier. That distance is what lets you see the whole mountain rather than looking up at its lower slopes.

faqs.q: Can I see Everest from Kala Patthar in the afternoon?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Afternoon cloud is common in the trekking seasons, but on settled days the summit stays clear until sunset. Mornings are more reliable. If you have only one chance, take the sunrise climb.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Kala Patthar?
faqs.a: No separate permit. Kala Patthar is inside Sagarmatha National Park, so the national park permit and the Khumbu Pasang Lhamu Rural Municipality permit cover it. Check current status of fees before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I fly to Kala Patthar by helicopter from Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Yes, on an Everest heli tour taking about 4–5 hours in total, including a refuelling stop at Lukla, a short landing on the ridge when permitted and breakfast at Hotel Everest View. Shared seats start around US$ 1,100–1,400 per person.

faqs.q: Is it safe to land at 5,550 m without acclimatisation?
faqs.a: For healthy adults, a 10–15 minute stop is generally fine, though mild headache or breathlessness is common. The danger rises with longer stays and pre-existing conditions. Tell the crew immediately if you feel faint, confused or very short of breath.
